items.stem: State what is meant by the term "complement of an event".
items.answer: The event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A bag has 2 red and 8 blue counters. Aiko says "there are only two colours, so P(red) = 1/2". Explain the mistake.
items.answer: The colours are not equally likely: P(red) = 2/10 = 1/5.
items.markingKey: Outcomes not equally likely (R1); correct probability (A1).

items.stem: Explain why the probability of getting a head on a fair coin is 1/2 even after five tails in a row.
items.answer: Each toss is independent; the coin has no memory, so the two outcomes are still equally likely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each toss is independent; the coin has no memory, so the two outcomes are still equally likely. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A fair 12-sided dice numbered 1 to 12 is rolled. Find the probability of rolling an odd number.
items.markingKey: Favourable outcomes 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 (M1); 6/12 = 1/2 (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "There are two outcomes – win or lose – so the probability of winning is 1/2." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The outcomes are not necessarily equally likely; probability depends on how many equally likely outcomes favour winning.
items.markingKey: The outcomes are not necessarily equally likely; probability depends on how many equally likely outcomes favour winning. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sectors: 3 are yellow and the rest are purple. (a) Find P(yellow) and P(purple). (b) Investigate how many sectors must be repainted yellow to make P(yellow) at least 3/4. (c) Explain why P(yellow) can never be 9/10 on this spinner.
items.answer: (a) 3/8, 5/8 (b) 3 (to make 6 yellow out of 8) (c) with 8 equal sectors every probability is a multiple of 1/8, and 9/10 is not
items.markingKey: (a) 3/8, 5/8 (b) 3 (to make 6 yellow out of 8) (c) with 8 equal sectors every probability is a multiple of 1/8, and 9/10 is not. Probabilities as fractions (A1 A1); equation or systematic trial (B: M1 A1); reasoned conclusion (R1).

items.stem: P(rain) = 0.35. What is P(no rain)?
Which term matches this description: "The event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A)"?
items.answer: complement of an event
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of complement of an event.

items.stem: Priya writes: "There are two outcomes – win or lose – so the probability of winning is 1/2." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The outcomes are not necessarily equally likely; probability depends on how many equally likely outcomes favour winning.
items.markingKey: The outcomes are not necessarily equally likely; probability depends on how many equally likely outcomes favour winning. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A bag has 2 red and 4 blue counters. Arjun says "there are only two colours, so P(red) = 1/2". Explain the mistake.
items.answer: The colours are not equally likely: P(red) = 2/6 = 1/3.
items.markingKey: Outcomes not equally likely (R1); correct probability (A1).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A probability of 0.7 means the event will happen 7 times." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It means the event is expected about 70% of the time in the long run; it is not a fixed count.
items.markingKey: It means the event is expected about 70% of the time in the long run; it is not a fixed count. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A jar contains 3 green, 2 black and 3 red sweets. One is chosen at random. Find (a) P(red or green), (b) P(not red).
A biased spinner lands on blue with probability 0.1, orange with 0.2 and red with 0.2. The only other colour is green. Find P(green).
items.markingKey: Probabilities add to 1 (R1); 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 (A1).

items.stem: A box contains 12 yellow, 5 black and 12 red counters. One is chosen at random. Find (a) P(black or red), (b) P(not black).

A bag contains 3 red and 3 blue marbles. (a) Find P(red). (b) Felix adds some red marbles so that P(red) becomes 8/11. How many were added? (c) How many blue marbles would have to be added instead (to the original bag) to make P(red) = 3/11?
items.markingKey: (a) 1/2 (b) 5 (c) 5. Probabilities as fractions (A1 A1); equation or systematic trial (B: M1 A1); reasoned conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A bag contains 6 red and 8 blue marbles. (a) Find P(red). (b) Mohammed adds some red marbles so that P(red) becomes 1/2. How many were added? (c) How many blue marbles would have to be added instead (to the original bag) to make P(red) = 3/8?
items.markingKey: (a) 3/7 (b) 2 (c) 2. Probabilities as fractions (A1 A1); equation or systematic trial (B: M1 A1); reasoned conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A grid or list showing every combined outcome of two events"?
items.answer: sample space diagram
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of sample space diagram.

items.stem: "When two dice are rolled, there are 11 possible totals, so P(total 7) = 1/11." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The 11 totals are not equally likely; out of 36 outcomes, 6 give 7, so P = 1/6.
items.markingKey: The 11 totals are not equally likely; out of 36 outcomes, 6 give 7, so P = 1/6. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf says that when two fair dice are rolled, a total of 3 is as likely as a total of 2. Explain why Yusuf is wrong, using the sample space.
items.answer: Total 3 can happen in 2 ways out of 36 but total 2 only in 1 way (1, 1), so P(3) = 1/18 > 1/36.
items.markingKey: Sample space of 36 used (M1); outcomes counted (A1); comparison (R1).

items.stem: A survey gave these results – boys: bus 12, walk 15, car 3; girls: bus 10, walk 4, car 7. One person is chosen at random. Find the probability that they are boys and chose bus.
Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. Draw a sample space diagram and find the probability that the total is greater than 4.
items.markingKey: 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes listed (M1); 30 favourable (A1); 5/6 (A1).

items.stem: A café in Kuala Lumpur offers a meal deal: one of 3 main courses and one of 3 drinks. (a) How many different meal deals are there? (b) List the sample space using letters. (c) If a deal is chosen at random, find the probability that it includes the first drink. (d) Explain how your answer to (a) would change if a choice of 2 desserts were added.
items.answer: (a) 9 (b) e.g. M1D1, M1D2, M1D3, … (c) 1/3 (d) it doubles to 18 (multiply by 2)
items.markingKey: (a) 9 (b) e.g. M1D1, M1D2, M1D3, … (c) 1/3 (d) it doubles to 18 (multiply by 2). Systematic sample space (M1 A1); probability (A1); fairness/change justified (R1 C1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "sample space diagram".
items.answer: A grid or list showing every combined outcome of two events
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a grid or list showing every combined outcome of two events. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a sample space diagram helps to find probabilities for two dice.
items.answer: It lists all 36 equally likely outcomes, so favourable outcomes can be counted without missing any.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It lists all 36 equally likely outcomes, so favourable outcomes can be counted without missing any. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Tossing two coins: P(one head and one tail) = 1/3, since outcomes are 2H, 2T or 1 each." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: There are four equally likely outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT; two give one of each, so P = 1/2.
items.markingKey: There are four equally likely outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT; two give one of each, so P = 1/2. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lukas says that when two fair dice are rolled, a total of 9 is as likely as a total of 2. Explain why Lukas is wrong, using the sample space.
items.answer: Total 9 can happen in 4 ways out of 36 but total 2 only in 1 way (1, 1), so P(9) = 1/9 > 1/36.
items.markingKey: Sample space of 36 used (M1); outcomes counted (A1); comparison (R1).

items.stem: A fair 6-sided dice and a fair 4-sided dice are rolled. Draw a sample space diagram and find the probability that the total is greater than 6.
items.markingKey: 6 × 4 = 24 outcomes listed (M1); 10 favourable (A1); 5/12 (A1).

items.stem: A survey gave these results – adults: cinema 8, museum 16, park 6; children: cinema 6, museum 10, park 6. Find (a) the probability that a randomly chosen person chose museum, (b) the probability that a person chosen from the adults chose museum.
items.markingKey: (a) column total 26/52 (M1 A1) (b) restricted to the row: 16/30 (M1 A1).

items.stem: Two fair 4-sided dice are rolled. Draw a sample space diagram and find the probability that the total is greater than 5.
items.markingKey: 4 × 4 = 16 outcomes listed (M1); 6 favourable (A1); 3/8 (A1).

items.stem: A survey gave these results – adults: cinema 6, museum 25, park 14; children: cinema 23, museum 13, park 17. Find (a) the probability that a randomly chosen person chose museum, (b) the probability that a person chosen from the children chose museum.
items.markingKey: (a) column total 38/98 (M1 A1) (b) restricted to the row: 13/53 (M1 A1).

items.stem: Mohammed and Kwame play a game with two fair six-sided dice. Mohammed wins if the difference between the scores is 0, 1 or 2; otherwise Kwame wins. (a) Draw a sample space diagram of the differences. (b) Find P(Mohammed wins). (c) Is the game fair? If not, suggest a change to make it fair.
items.answer: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Mohammed wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair
items.markingKey: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Mohammed wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair. Systematic sample space (M1 A1); probability (A1); fairness/change justified (R1 C1).

items.stem: Leila and Mohammed play a game with two fair six-sided dice. Leila wins if the difference between the scores is 0, 1 or 2; otherwise Mohammed wins. (a) Draw a sample space diagram of the differences. (b) Find P(Leila wins). (c) Is the game fair? If not, suggest a change to make it fair.
items.answer: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Leila wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair
items.markingKey: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Leila wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair. Systematic sample space (M1 A1); probability (A1); fairness/change justified (R1 C1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A probability estimated from the results of an experiment or survey"?
items.answer: experimental probability
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of experimental probability.

items.stem: A student claims: "After 100 rolls, a fair dice must have shown exactly 50 even numbers." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: You expect about 50, but random variation means the actual number will usually be a little different.
items.markingKey: You expect about 50, but random variation means the actual number will usually be a little different. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf rolls a dice 30 times and gets 11 sixes. Jonas rolls the same dice 400 times and gets 98 sixes. Explain whose results give the better estimate of P(six), and give that estimate.
items.answer: Jonas’s, because 400 trials is many more than 30; estimate 98/400 = 0.245.
items.markingKey: More trials more reliable (R1); estimate (A1).

items.stem: A dice is rolled 180 times with results 1: 25, 2: 34, 3: 37, 4: 23, 5: 36, 6: 25. (a) Find the relative frequency of a 3. (b) How many of each score would you expect from a fair dice? (c) Comment on whether the dice appears biased.
items.answer: (a) 37/180 ≈ 0.206 (b) 30 each (c) the 3 differs noticeably from 30, which suggests possible bias; more trials would help
items.markingKey: (a) 37/180 (A1); (b) 180/6 = 30 (A1); (c) comparison with expected frequencies and a sensible conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Mateo throws a bottle-flip 400 times; it lands upright 187 times. (a) Estimate the probability that it lands upright. (b) Estimate how many times it would land upright in 500 throws.

Jonas tests a home-made spinner and records the number of times it lands on green after 10, 50, 100, 200 and 500 spins (cumulative totals): 1, 16, 21, 44, 130. (a) Calculate the relative frequency after each number of spins. (b) Describe what happens to the relative frequency. (c) Give the best estimate of P(green) and explain your choice. (d) Estimate the number of greens in 2000 spins.
items.answer: (a) 0.1, 0.32, 0.21, 0.22, 0.26 (b) it varies a lot at first and then settles down (c) 0.26, from the largest number of trials (d) about 520
items.markingKey: Relative frequencies (M1 A1); trend described (B: R1); best estimate justified (R1); expected number (A1); communication (C1).

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed 50 times and gives 31 heads. This means:
options: the next toss will be a tail
the result is possible for a fair coin; more trials are needed to judge
items.answer: the result is possible for a fair coin; more trials are needed to judge
items.markingKey: C. Random variation is expected in small samples.

items.stem: Explain when you would use experimental probability rather than theoretical probability.
items.answer: When outcomes are not equally likely or cannot be calculated, e.g. a biased dice or the chance of rain; you estimate from repeated trials or data.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When outcomes are not equally likely or cannot be calculated, e.g. a biased dice or the chance of rain; you estimate from repeated trials or data. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Rafael rolls a dice 30 times and gets 12 sixes. Sana rolls the same dice 500 times and gets 95 sixes. Explain whose results give the better estimate of P(six), and give that estimate.
items.answer: Sana’s, because 500 trials is many more than 30; estimate 95/500 = 0.19.
items.markingKey: More trials more reliable (R1); estimate (A1).

items.stem: Omar rolls a dice 40 times and gets 5 sixes. Felix rolls the same dice 1000 times and gets 126 sixes. Explain whose results give the better estimate of P(six), and give that estimate.
items.answer: Felix’s, because 1000 trials is many more than 40; estimate 126/1000 = 0.126.
items.markingKey: More trials more reliable (R1); estimate (A1).

items.stem: A dice is rolled 300 times with results 1: 47, 2: 45, 3: 51, 4: 60, 5: 48, 6: 49. (a) Find the relative frequency of a 4. (b) How many of each score would you expect from a fair dice? (c) Comment on whether the dice appears biased.
items.answer: (a) 1/5 ≈ 0.200 (b) 50 each (c) the frequencies are close to 50, so there is no strong evidence of bias
items.markingKey: (a) 60/300 (A1); (b) 300/6 = 50 (A1); (c) comparison with expected frequencies and a sensible conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Arjun throws a drawing pin 50 times; it lands point up 42 times. (a) Estimate the probability that it lands point up. (b) Estimate how many times it would land point up in 500 throws.

A dice is rolled 180 times with results 1: 32, 2: 27, 3: 37, 4: 28, 5: 24, 6: 32. (a) Find the relative frequency of a 3. (b) How many of each score would you expect from a fair dice? (c) Comment on whether the dice appears biased.
items.answer: (a) 37/180 ≈ 0.206 (b) 30 each (c) the 3 differs noticeably from 30, which suggests possible bias; more trials would help
items.markingKey: (a) 37/180 (A1); (b) 180/6 = 30 (A1); (c) comparison with expected frequencies and a sensible conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Leila throws a biased coin 120 times; it shows heads 75 times. (a) Estimate the probability that it shows heads. (b) Estimate how many times it would show heads in 2000 throws.

Nia tests a home-made spinner and records the number of times it lands on green after 10, 50, 100, 200 and 500 spins (cumulative totals): 3, 22, 42, 87, 205. (a) Calculate the relative frequency after each number of spins. (b) Describe what happens to the relative frequency. (c) Give the best estimate of P(green) and explain your choice. (d) Estimate the number of greens in 2000 spins.
items.answer: (a) 0.3, 0.44, 0.42, 0.435, 0.41 (b) it varies a lot at first and then settles down (c) 0.41, from the largest number of trials (d) about 820
items.markingKey: Relative frequencies (M1 A1); trend described (B: R1); best estimate justified (R1); expected number (A1); communication (C1).

items.stem: Hana tests a home-made spinner and records the number of times it lands on green after 10, 50, 100, 200 and 500 spins (cumulative totals): 2, 18, 32, 57, 140. (a) Calculate the relative frequency after each number of spins. (b) Describe what happens to the relative frequency. (c) Give the best estimate of P(green) and explain your choice. (d) Estimate the number of greens in 2000 spins.
items.answer: (a) 0.2, 0.36, 0.32, 0.285, 0.28 (b) it varies a lot at first and then settles down (c) 0.28, from the largest number of trials (d) about 560
items.markingKey: Relative frequencies (M1 A1); trend described (B: R1); best estimate justified (R1); expected number (A1); communication (C1).

items.stem: Define the term "expected frequency".
items.answer: The number of times an outcome is expected: probability × number of trials
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number of times an outcome is expected: probability × number of trials. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Aiko tosses two coins. Aiko scores a point for two heads; Leila scores a point for one head and one tail. Explain whether the game is fair.
items.answer: Not fair: P(two heads) = 1/4 but P(one of each) = 2/4 = 1/2, so the second player is twice as likely to score.
items.markingKey: Four outcomes listed (M1); probabilities (A1); conclusion (R1).

items.stem: "A game where you win on a 6 and lose otherwise is fair because there are two results." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: P(win) = 1/6 and P(lose) = 5/6, so the game is not fair.
items.markingKey: P(win) = 1/6 and P(lose) = 5/6, so the game is not fair. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: At a school fair in Toronto it costs C$2 to roll a fair dice. If you roll a 5 or a 6, you win C$4 (and your stake is kept by the stall). (a) Find the expected profit or loss for the stall from 60 games. (b) Is the game fair for the player? Explain.
items.answer: (a) stall takes C$120, expected pay-out C$80: profit C$40 (b) not fair – the expected gain per game for the player is negative
items.markingKey: Expected wins 1/3 × 60 = 20 (M1 A1); money in vs money out (M1 A1); conclusion on fairness (R1).

items.stem: A charity stall in Lisbon charges €1 per game. Players spin a fair spinner with 10 equal sections. (a) Design prizes so that the stall expects to make a profit of about €50 from 200 games, showing your calculations. (b) Explain why the stall could still lose money on a particular day. (c) Explain whether your game is fair to the players.
items.answer: (a) e.g. 1 winning section with a prize of €7.50: expected pay-out per game €0.75, profit €0.25 per game × 200 = €50 (b) the results are random; more winners than expected can occur (c) not fair – the player’s expected gain is negative (that is how the charity raises money)
items.markingKey: Expected pay-out calculated (M1 A1); profit target met (A1); variability explained (R1); fairness discussed (R1 C1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fair game"?
options: A grid or list showing every combined outcome of two events
A probability estimated from the results of an experiment or survey
A game in which every player has the same chance of winning (or the expected gain is zero)
The event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
items.answer: A game in which every player has the same chance of winning (or the expected gain is zero)
items.markingKey: C. "fair game" is a game in which every player has the same chance of winning (or the expected gain is zero).

items.stem: Explain how you can decide whether a game is fair.
items.answer: Work out each player’s probability of winning (or expected gain); the game is fair if they are equal (or the expected gain is zero).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Work out each player’s probability of winning (or expected gain); the game is fair if they are equal (or the expected gain is zero). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "If P(rain) = 0.2, it will rain on exactly 6 days in a 30-day month." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Expected number is 0.2 × 30 = 6, but the actual number can vary.
items.markingKey: Expected number is 0.2 × 30 = 6, but the actual number can vary. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A fair spinner has 10 equal sections, 3 of which are blue. It is spun 60 times. Find the expected number of blues.
A fair six-sided dice is rolled 300 times. How many times would you expect to roll a number greater than 4?

(a) Design prizes so that the stall expects to make a profit of about RM100 from 200 games, showing your calculations. (b) Explain why the stall could still lose money on a particular day. (c) Explain whether your game is fair to the players.
items.answer: (a) e.g. 1 winning section with a prize of RM15.00: expected pay-out per game RM1.50, profit RM0.50 per game × 200 = RM100 (b) the results are random; more winners than expected can occur (c) not fair – the player’s expected gain is negative (that is how the charity raises money)
items.markingKey: Expected pay-out calculated (M1 A1); profit target met (A1); variability explained (R1); fairness discussed (R1 C1).

items.stem: A charity stall in Geneva charges CHF 2 per game. Players spin a fair spinner with 10 equal sections. items.answer: (a) e.g. 1 winning section with a prize of CHF 15.00: expected pay-out per game CHF 1.50, profit CHF 0.50 per game × 100 = CHF 50 (b) the results are random; more winners than expected can occur (c) not fair – the player’s expected gain is negative (that is how the charity raises money)
items.markingKey: Expected pay-out calculated (M1 A1); profit target met (A1); variability explained (R1); fairness discussed (R1 C1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "complement of an event"?
options: The event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
Outcomes that each have the same chance of happening
A table that shows the frequencies of two categorical variables at the same time
A number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is to happen
items.answer: The event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
items.markingKey: A. "complement of an event" is the event "A does not happen", with P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sample space"?
options: A probability estimated from the results of an experiment or survey
One performance of an experiment, such as one roll of a dice
Not fair: some outcomes are more likely than they should be
The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment
items.answer: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment
items.markingKey: D. "sample space" is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.

items.stem: Define the term "trial".
items.answer: One performance of an experiment, such as one roll of a dice
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: one performance of an experiment, such as one roll of a dice. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a fairground stall that charges to play is usually not a fair game for the player.
items.answer: The prizes are set so that, on average, the stall takes in more money than it pays out; the player’s expected gain is negative.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The prizes are set so that, on average, the stall takes in more money than it pays out; the player’s expected gain is negative. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why P(A) + P(not A) = 1.
items.answer: Every outcome is either in A or not in A, and not both, so the two probabilities together cover all outcomes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every outcome is either in A or not in A, and not both, so the two probabilities together cover all outcomes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ingrid says that when two fair dice are rolled, a total of 10 is as likely as a total of 2. Explain why Ingrid is wrong, using the sample space.
items.answer: Total 10 can happen in 3 ways out of 36 but total 2 only in 1 way (1, 1), so P(10) = 1/12 > 1/36.
items.markingKey: Sample space of 36 used (M1); outcomes counted (A1); comparison (R1).

items.stem: Sofia rolls a dice 20 times and gets 8 sixes. Leila rolls the same dice 500 times and gets 76 sixes. Explain whose results give the better estimate of P(six), and give that estimate.
items.answer: Leila’s, because 500 trials is many more than 20; estimate 76/500 = 0.152.
items.markingKey: More trials more reliable (R1); estimate (A1).

items.stem: Elena and Lukas roll two dice. Elena wins if the total is even and Lukas wins if it is odd. Explain whether this game is fair.
items.answer: Fair: 18 of the 36 outcomes give an even total and 18 give an odd total, so each has probability 1/2.
items.markingKey: Sample space used (M1); counts 18 and 18 (A1); conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A bag has 4 red and 7 blue counters. Hana says "there are only two colours, so P(red) = 1/2". Explain the mistake.
items.answer: The colours are not equally likely: P(red) = 4/11 = 4/11.
items.markingKey: Outcomes not equally likely (R1); correct probability (A1).

items.markingKey: There are four equally likely outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT; two give one of each, so P = 1/2. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: At a school fair in Melbourne it costs A$1 to roll a fair dice. If you roll a 5 or a 6, you win A$5 (and your stake is kept by the stall). (a) Find the expected profit or loss for the stall from 120 games. (b) Is the game fair for the player? Explain.
items.answer: (a) stall takes A$120, expected pay-out A$200: loss A$80 (b) not fair – the expected gain per game for the player is positive
items.markingKey: Expected wins 1/3 × 120 = 40 (M1 A1); money in vs money out (M1 A1); conclusion on fairness (R1).

items.stem: A box contains 3 black, 3 green and 5 blue marbles. One is chosen at random. Find (a) P(blue or black), (b) P(not blue).

A survey gave these results – adults: cinema 25, museum 6, park 7; children: cinema 4, museum 13, park 23. Find (a) the probability that a randomly chosen person chose museum, (b) the probability that a person chosen from the adults chose museum.
items.markingKey: (a) column total 19/78 (M1 A1) (b) restricted to the row: 6/38 (M1 A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "A dice landed on 6 three times in 10 rolls, so P(6) = 3/10 exactly." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: 3/10 is only an estimate from a small number of trials; the theoretical probability for a fair dice is 1/6.
items.markingKey: 3/10 is only an estimate from a small number of trials; the theoretical probability for a fair dice is 1/6. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: At a school fair in Vienna it costs €2 to roll a fair dice. If you roll a 6, you win €4 (and your stake is kept by the stall). (a) Find the expected profit or loss for the stall from 60 games. (b) Is the game fair for the player? Explain.
items.answer: (a) stall takes €120, expected pay-out €40: profit €80 (b) not fair – the expected gain per game for the player is negative
items.markingKey: Expected wins 1/6 × 60 = 10 (M1 A1); money in vs money out (M1 A1); conclusion on fairness (R1).

items.stem: A bag contains 2 red and 5 blue marbles. (a) Find P(red). (b) Sofia adds some red marbles so that P(red) becomes 6/11. How many were added? (c) How many blue marbles would have to be added instead (to the original bag) to make P(red) = 2/11?
items.markingKey: (a) 2/7 (b) 4 (c) 4. Probabilities as fractions (A1 A1); equation or systematic trial (B: M1 A1); reasoned conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Elena and Priya play a game with two fair six-sided dice. Elena wins if the difference between the scores is 0, 1 or 2; otherwise Priya wins. (a) Draw a sample space diagram of the differences. (b) Find P(Elena wins). (c) Is the game fair? If not, suggest a change to make it fair.
items.answer: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Elena wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair
items.markingKey: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Elena wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair. Systematic sample space (M1 A1); probability (A1); fairness/change justified (R1 C1).

items.stem: Arjun tests a home-made spinner and records the number of times it lands on green after 10, 50, 100, 200 and 500 spins (cumulative totals): 1, 9, 21, 53, 125. (a) Calculate the relative frequency after each number of spins. (b) Describe what happens to the relative frequency. (c) Give the best estimate of P(green) and explain your choice. (d) Estimate the number of greens in 2000 spins.
items.answer: (a) 0.1, 0.18, 0.21, 0.265, 0.25 (b) it varies a lot at first and then settles down (c) 0.25, from the largest number of trials (d) about 500
items.markingKey: Relative frequencies (M1 A1); trend described (B: R1); best estimate justified (R1); expected number (A1); communication (C1).

items.stem: A charity stall in Accra charges GH₵3 per game. Players spin a fair spinner with 10 equal sections. (a) Design prizes so that the stall expects to make a profit of about GH₵225 from 300 games, showing your calculations. (b) Explain why the stall could still lose money on a particular day. (c) Explain whether your game is fair to the players.
items.answer: (a) e.g. 1 winning section with a prize of GH₵22.50: expected pay-out per game GH₵2.25, profit GH₵0.75 per game × 300 = GH₵225 (b) the results are random; more winners than expected can occur (c) not fair – the player’s expected gain is negative (that is how the charity raises money)
items.markingKey: Expected pay-out calculated (M1 A1); profit target met (A1); variability explained (R1); fairness discussed (R1 C1).

items.stem: Which word best describes the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair dice?
items.answer: unlikely
items.markingKey: A. Rolling a 6 on a fair dice is unlikely.

items.stem: What is the probability of getting two heads when two fair coins are tossed?
items.markingKey: B. HH is 1 of 4 outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT.

items.stem: A spinner lands on red 33 times in 80 spins. What is the relative frequency of red?
Sofia and Isabel roll two dice. Sofia wins if the total is even and Isabel wins if it is odd. Explain whether this game is fair.
items.answer: Fair: 18 of the 36 outcomes give an even total and 18 give an odd total, so each has probability 1/2.
items.markingKey: Sample space used (M1); counts 18 and 18 (A1); conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A student claims: "A probability of 0.7 means the event will happen 7 times." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It means the event is expected about 70% of the time in the long run; it is not a fixed count.
items.markingKey: It means the event is expected about 70% of the time in the long run; it is not a fixed count. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why HT and TH must be counted as different outcomes when two coins are tossed.
items.answer: The coins are different (first and second), so "head then tail" and "tail then head" are separate equally likely outcomes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The coins are different (first and second), so "head then tail" and "tail then head" are separate equally likely outcomes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability as the number of trials increases.
items.answer: Random variations even out over many trials (the law of large numbers), so the proportion settles towards the true probability.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random variations even out over many trials (the law of large numbers), so the proportion settles towards the true probability. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the expected number of sixes in 60 rolls is 10, even though you might not get exactly 10.
items.answer: Expected frequency = 1/6 × 60 = 10 is the long-run average; random variation means the actual count usually differs slightly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Expected frequency = 1/6 × 60 = 10 is the long-run average; random variation means the actual count usually differs slightly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A bag has 5 red and 6 blue counters. Noah says "there are only two colours, so P(red) = 1/2". Explain the mistake.
items.answer: The colours are not equally likely: P(red) = 5/11 = 5/11.
items.markingKey: Outcomes not equally likely (R1); correct probability (A1).

items.stem: A fair 4-sided dice and a fair 6-sided dice are rolled. Draw a sample space diagram and find the probability that the product is even.
items.markingKey: 4 × 6 = 24 outcomes listed (M1); 18 favourable (A1); 3/4 (A1).

items.stem: A dice is rolled 120 times with results 1: 20, 2: 18, 3: 25, 4: 25, 5: 18, 6: 14. (a) Find the relative frequency of a 6. (b) How many of each score would you expect from a fair dice? (c) Comment on whether the dice appears biased.
items.answer: (a) 7/60 ≈ 0.117 (b) 20 each (c) the 6 differs noticeably from 20, which suggests possible bias; more trials would help
items.markingKey: (a) 14/120 (A1); (b) 120/6 = 20 (A1); (c) comparison with expected frequencies and a sensible conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A fair six-sided dice is rolled 300 times. How many times would you expect to roll a 1 or a 2?
A bag contains 6 white, 6 black and 7 yellow marbles. One is chosen at random. Find (a) P(white or black), (b) P(not white).
A student claims: "When two dice are rolled, there are 11 possible totals, so P(total 7) = 1/11." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The 11 totals are not equally likely; out of 36 outcomes, 6 give 7, so P = 1/6.
items.markingKey: The 11 totals are not equally likely; out of 36 outcomes, 6 give 7, so P = 1/6. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A dice is rolled 300 times with results 1: 50, 2: 49, 3: 57, 4: 54, 5: 51, 6: 39. (a) Find the relative frequency of a 6. (b) How many of each score would you expect from a fair dice? (c) Comment on whether the dice appears biased.
items.answer: (a) 13/100 ≈ 0.130 (b) 50 each (c) the 6 differs noticeably from 50, which suggests possible bias; more trials would help
items.markingKey: (a) 39/300 (A1); (b) 300/6 = 50 (A1); (c) comparison with expected frequencies and a sensible conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A fair six-sided dice is rolled 180 times. How many times would you expect to roll a 6?

A bag contains 2 red and 7 blue marbles. (a) Find P(red). (b) Lars adds some red marbles so that P(red) becomes 8/15. How many were added? (c) How many blue marbles would have to be added instead (to the original bag) to make P(red) = 2/15?
items.markingKey: (a) 2/9 (b) 6 (c) 6. Probabilities as fractions (A1 A1); equation or systematic trial (B: M1 A1); reasoned conclusion (R1).

items.markingKey: (a) a 6 × 6 grid of differences (b) 24/36 = 2/3 (c) not fair; e.g. Maya wins only on a difference of 1 or 2 (10 + 8 = 18 outcomes, 18/36 = 1/2), which is fair. Systematic sample space (M1 A1); probability (A1); fairness/change justified (R1 C1).

items.stem: Lukas tests a home-made spinner and records the number of times it lands on green after 10, 50, 100, 200 and 500 spins (cumulative totals): 4, 17, 28, 63, 145. (a) Calculate the relative frequency after each number of spins. (b) Describe what happens to the relative frequency. (c) Give the best estimate of P(green) and explain your choice. (d) Estimate the number of greens in 2000 spins.
items.answer: (a) 0.4, 0.34, 0.28, 0.315, 0.29 (b) it varies a lot at first and then settles down (c) 0.29, from the largest number of trials (d) about 580
items.markingKey: Relative frequencies (M1 A1); trend described (B: R1); best estimate justified (R1); expected number (A1); communication (C1).

items.stem: A charity stall in Dubai charges AED 1 per game. Players spin a fair spinner with 10 equal sections. (a) Design prizes so that the stall expects to make a profit of about AED 75 from 300 games, showing your calculations. (b) Explain why the stall could still lose money on a particular day. (c) Explain whether your game is fair to the players.
items.answer: (a) e.g. 1 winning section with a prize of AED 7.50: expected pay-out per game AED 0.75, profit AED 0.25 per game × 300 = AED 75 (b) the results are random; more winners than expected can occur (c) not fair – the player’s expected gain is negative (that is how the charity raises money)
items.markingKey: Expected pay-out calculated (M1 A1); profit target met (A1); variability explained (R1); fairness discussed (R1 C1).
